passage:
Hi Francis,
You asked why I'm still doing the phone-cover printing thing. Honest answer: I can't bear to call it a loss. Eight months, the printer, the stock under my bed, and we've sold maybe forty covers. Every week I tell myself one more push and it'll turn. If I stop, then it's official that I wasted all that.
The funny part? The maths tutoring I started in January was actually working. Six kids, good feedback, parents asking for more slots. I quit it in March because I'd "had enough" and wanted time for the covers. I think I just wanted to lock in the win before it could go wrong.
Writing this down, it sounds backwards, doesn't it? Tell me honestly.
Pankaj

qa.q: How many covers has Pankaj sold in eight months?
qa.a: Maybe forty covers.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj keep going with the phone covers?
qa.a: Pankaj is afraid of the hurt of calling it a loss, so stopping feels like making the waste official, and hoping feels safer than admitting it.

qa.q: What would you advise Pankaj to think about?
qa.a: Judge each project by how it is likely to go from here, not by what is already spent, and look again at the tutoring that was working.

qa.q: How might Francis read this letter?
qa.a: Francis may feel glad Pankaj is being honest, and could gently agree that holding the failing project while dropping the working one sounds backwards.

grounding: A young adult keeps a failing side project going to avoid admitting the loss, after quitting a successful one early.

passage: Noor, you'll laugh, but I finally see what Disha does. Two years ago I started two things at college: the quiz club and the film society. The quiz club took off: sixty members, an inter-college win. And the moment it was doing well, I handed it to a junior. I told myself I'd done my part. I think I was scared it would fall and my win would go with it. The film society? Four people come, and one of them is me. The projector is broken. I've kept it going for two years, booking the room, making posters, because shutting it means saying out loud that it failed. Holding the bad one, letting go of the good one early. It's like I'm protecting myself from a feeling, not making a decision.

qa.q: How many members did the quiz club have?
qa.a: Sixty members.

qa.q: Why has Disha kept the film society going for two years?
qa.a: Disha dreads the hurt of admitting it failed, so booking rooms and making posters feels easier than saying it out loud.

qa.q: What question could help Disha decide about the film society?
qa.a: Whether Disha would start it today, with four members and a broken projector; if not, it may be time to close it and put energy where things work.

qa.q: What would change if Disha had kept leading the quiz club?
qa.a: The club might have grown further with Disha's energy, instead of that energy going into a society four people attend.

grounding: A student describes handing off a thriving club too soon while keeping a failing one alive to avoid admitting the loss.

passage:
Monday. Wasim's final-year project app still crashed on login, eight weeks in. Mridul, his teammate, suggested switching to the simple attendance tool they'd built in week two, the one that already worked. "We dropped that because it was too easy," Wasim said. "This one is ours now. We can't just throw eight weeks away."
Thursday. Another all-nighter. The login crashed again at 3 a.m. Wasim stared at the screen, eyes burning, and still said, "One more week and it'll work."
Saturday. Their guide looked at both. "The attendance tool works and the department actually needs it. The other one needs three more months." Wasim went quiet for a long time. Then he opened the old folder. "Okay. We finish the one that works." Mridul let out a breath he had been holding for weeks.

qa.q: How long had the team been working on the app?
qa.a: Eight weeks.

qa.q: Why did Wasim refuse to switch on Monday?
qa.a: He felt he couldn't bear to throw away eight weeks, so calling the app a loss hurt more than struggling on with it.

qa.q: What helped Wasim change course, and why?
qa.a: The guide comparing both projects plainly, which made Wasim judge what would work from now on rather than what had been spent.

qa.q: What was the week like for Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul was probably frustrated and tired, holding his breath for weeks while the working tool sat unused.

grounding: Over a week, a student clings to a failing project to avoid admitting the loss, after setting aside a working one too early.

passage:
Operations manager's note, warehouse team, Nagpur, 5 June
We needed to move the team from fixed Saturday offs to a rotating off-day. Last year, when I proposed something similar, the team saw only what they'd lose and refused. This time Deepak, one of our shift leads, asked to present it. He had noticed that people argued far harder to hold on to something they already had than to win something new. So he started with what stays protected: "Everyone keeps two offs a week, and nobody works more than five days in a row." Then he was honest about the cost: "Some of you will lose your fixed Saturday." Aditi asked who. He showed the list. There was grumbling, but no walk-out, and the team voted to try it for one month.

qa.q: How many offs a week does everyone keep?
qa.a: Two offs a week.

qa.q: Why did Deepak start with what stays protected?
qa.a: He felt concerned that people would fight to keep what they had, so he wanted them to feel safe about what wasn't changing before hearing the cost.

qa.q: Why was it important that Deepak named what would be lost?
qa.a: Being honest about losing the fixed Saturday built trust, so the team could weigh the change fairly instead of feeling tricked.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel when she sees the list?
qa.a: Aditi may feel uneasy if her name is on it, but respected that she was shown the truth instead of hidden changes.

grounding: A manager records a young shift lead who noticed people fight to keep benefits, so he framed a change by what is protected and admitted what is lost.

passage:
Tuesday
The canteen meeting went better than last time. HR's first plan was to swap the free lunch for a meal allowance of the same value. Everyone heard only "losing free lunch" and nearly revolted, even though the value was equal.
Today Rajni from HR let me speak. I'd noticed people defend a benefit much harder than they chase a new one. So I started with what stays: "Nobody loses a meal. The canteen stays open, same hours, same tea." Then the honest part: "What changes is that lunch isn't automatic. You get the allowance and choose where to eat. Some of you will miss the free thali. That's real." People still grumbled. But they asked questions instead of shouting.
Yogesh

qa.q: What stays the same, according to Yogesh?
qa.a: The canteen stays open, same hours, same tea.

qa.q: How did Yogesh seem to feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Yogesh seemed relieved and a little pleased that people asked questions instead of shouting.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's way of presenting fairer than HR's first plan?
qa.a: It began with what was protected and openly admitted what would be missed, so people felt safe enough to discuss it.

qa.q: How might Rajni see Yogesh's approach?
qa.a: Rajni probably feels grateful and relieved, since a change that nearly caused a revolt was discussed calmly.

grounding: A young employee who noticed people defend benefits harder than they seek new ones frames a change by what is kept and admits what is lost.

passage: Indu, you're scared to take the Bengaluru posting because of what you'd give up here. Let your old Vandana ma'am tell you what I did at twenty-five. The bank offered me a transfer to a new branch, a bigger role. All I could think about was losing: my flat near Amma, my evening walks with friends, my known desk. So one night I sat with a notebook and wrote two lines of the same size. "I lose my evening walks with friends." "I gain a team of my own to lead." Then I asked myself: if both were offered fresh, which would I truly want? Side by side, the loss didn't look so huge. I took the transfer. I missed the walks, honestly. But I never regretted it.

qa.q: What did the bank offer young Vandana?
qa.a: A transfer to a new branch, with a bigger role.

qa.q: What was young Vandana feeling before she wrote the two lines?
qa.a: She felt afraid of losing her flat near Amma, her walks and her known desk, so the safe option seemed like the only one.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vandana's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Writing a loss and a gain of the same size side by side and asking which she would truly want; it shrank the automatic pull toward staying.

qa.q: How might Vandana's friends have felt about her leaving?
qa.a: They probably missed the evening walks too, and may have felt sad but proud of her new role.

grounding: A senior woman recalls writing an equal loss and gain side by side to decide on a transfer, easing her pull toward the safe option.

passage: The fellowship office wanted an answer by 9 p.m., and at seven the power went out across Lavanya's lane. By candlelight, her phone at eleven percent, she sat with Charu on the steps. "Every time I think of it, I just see what I'd lose," Lavanya said. "The permanent post. Everyone saying I threw it away." Charu handed her a notebook. "Then make them the same size. Write one real loss and one real gain." Lavanya wrote: "I give up two years in a permanent job." Then: "I gain two years of work I actually believe in." She looked at the two lines in the flickering light. "If someone offered me either one fresh, which would I pick?" The answer came quicker than she expected. At 8:47 she typed yes, with four percent battery left.

qa.q: How much battery was left when Lavanya typed yes?
qa.a: Four percent.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling before Charu handed her the notebook?
qa.a: She felt anxious and stuck, seeing only the losses: the permanent post and people saying she threw it away.

qa.q: What did the two-line exercise do for Lavanya?
qa.a: Writing a loss and a gain of the same size and asking which she would pick fresh eased the automatic pull toward the safe job.

qa.q: What is it like for Charu to sit with Lavanya in the power cut?
qa.a: Charu seems calm and caring, offering a simple tool rather than telling Lavanya what to choose.

grounding: Under a deadline and a power cut, a young woman writes an equal loss and gain side by side and asks which she would truly prefer.

passage: Afreen had been saying "maybe next month" about the Gomti Nagar flat for four months. Her office was there; her family home in the old city was an hour and a half away each side. On Sunday her sister Mehak found her circling the listing again. "What's stopping you?" "I'll lose Ammi's cooking. My room. The neighbourhood." Mehak took a pen. "Now the other side, same size." Afreen thought. "I gain three hours a day." She wrote both lines on the back of an electricity bill and stared. "If I lived in Gomti Nagar already, would I move somewhere that added three hours of travel just for my old room?" "Would you?" Afreen laughed. "No." She messaged the owner that evening, and promised Ammi every Sunday lunch.

qa.q: How long was Afreen's commute each way?
qa.a: An hour and a half each side.

qa.q: Why had Afreen kept saying maybe next month?
qa.a: She felt afraid of losing Ammi's cooking, her room and the neighbourhood, so staying felt safer even though the flat made sense.

qa.q: What question helped Afreen see the choice evenly?
qa.a: Whether, if she already lived near work, she would move somewhere that added three hours of travel just for her old room.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel about Afreen's promise?
qa.a: Ammi may feel sad to see her go but comforted by the promise of every Sunday lunch.

grounding: A young woman writes a loss and a gain of equal size and flips the question around, easing her pull toward staying put.

passage: In the building's play area, Omkar held a small red toy car he had got free with a cereal box that morning. Tarun had a blue car, exactly the same size. "Swap?" Tarun asked. "Just for today?" Omkar hugged the red car to his chest. "No! Mine is faster. Mine is the best one." "They're the same," Tarun said, holding his up. Omkar shook his head hard and hid the car behind his back, though yesterday he hadn't known it existed.

qa.q: What colour was Tarun's car?
qa.a: Blue, exactly the same size.

qa.q: Why does Omkar say his red car is faster?
qa.a: He feels proud and protective because it is his now, so it seems more special than Tarun's, even though they are the same.

qa.q: How could a grown-up help with the swap?
qa.a: They could let both boys race the two cars side by side, then offer a short swap with a promise that Omkar gets his car back.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel when Omkar hides the car?
qa.a: Tarun may feel disappointed and a little puzzled, since his car is just the same.

grounding: A young boy refuses a fair swap because a car he got that morning now feels far more precious simply because it is his.

passage:
"Raghav, this teddy's ear is torn. Shall we give it away and get you the new yellow one from the shop?" Neelam asked.
"NO!" Raghav grabbed the old brown teddy. "Mine!"
"The yellow one is soft and new. Same size."
"Mine is softer."
"It's torn, beta."
"Mine is torn best."
Neelam laughed. "Okay. Want to see the yellow one anyway?"
Raghav peeped at it, then pressed his face into the brown teddy. "Yellow one is for other boys."

qa.q: What was wrong with Raghav's old teddy?
qa.a: Its ear was torn.

qa.q: Why does Raghav say his torn teddy is softer?
qa.a: He feels attached and protective because it is his, so it seems better than the new yellow one, even torn.

qa.q: What could Neelam try if the teddy really must be replaced?
qa.a: Stitch the ear, or let Raghav keep the old teddy while the new one visits for a few days, so nothing is taken from him suddenly.

qa.q: How does Neelam seem to feel about Raghav's answer?
qa.a: Neelam seems amused and gentle, laughing rather than forcing the swap.

grounding: A young boy insists his own torn teddy is better than an equal new one, simply because it is his.

passage:
Nursery teacher's note, Tuesday
At sand time, Yash picked the green spade from the basket. Ten minutes later Vaibhav offered him the orange spade, the same kind, so he could try green. Yash held the green one tight and said, "Mine is the good one. Yours is broken." It was not broken. When I asked, he said green "digs more." I gave both boys a bucket and had them race to fill it. They filled them at the same time. Yash kept the green spade, but let Vaibhav hold it for one turn.

qa.q: What colour spade did Vaibhav offer Yash?
qa.a: The orange spade, the same kind.

qa.q: Why did Yash say the orange spade was broken?
qa.a: He felt protective of the green spade because it was his, so the other one seemed worse, even though it was not broken.

qa.q: Why was the bucket race a good idea?
qa.a: It let Yash see both spades dig the same, without forcing him to hand over his.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel when Yash calls his spade broken?
qa.a: Vaibhav might feel a bit hurt or confused, since he offered a fair swap and his spade worked fine.

grounding: A nursery teacher records a young boy refusing a fair swap because the spade he picked now feels better simply for being his.

passage:
Wednesday
Jasleen wanted my Golden Bowler card today. She offered three normal cards for it. THREE. I said ten or nothing. She said, "Nobody gives ten, Yogesh. It's not even that rare. Bunty has two." I said she was trying to cheat me because I'm younger. Then she went and traded with Bunty for three cards, and he was happy.
Now I'm annoyed. My Golden Bowler is shiny, and I've had it since my birthday. It feels like it's worth at least ten. But when I wanted Bunty's Flying Keeper last month, I only offered two, and I thought HE was greedy for saying no.
Hmm.
Yogesh

qa.q: How many cards did Jasleen offer for the Golden Bowler?
qa.a: Three normal cards.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh think Jasleen was trying to cheat?
qa.a: Yogesh feels the card is worth at least ten because it is shiny and owned since a birthday, so a fair offer felt like an insult.

qa.q: What could Yogesh check before the next trade?
qa.a: What other kids usually give for that card, like Bunty's trade for three, and whether Yogesh would pay ten to get it.

qa.q: How did Bunty feel about his trade with Jasleen?
qa.a: Bunty was happy trading his card for three, which shows three was a fair offer.

grounding: A child's diary shows demanding far more for an owned card than others will give, and calling a fair offer cheating.

passage: On the dusty ground behind the village school, Yusuf spun his old wooden top, the one with the chipped red stripe. Devika watched. "I'll give you my new paper kite for it," she said. It was a good kite, with a long tail. Yusuf snorted. "This top is worth your kite AND your marbles." "It's chipped!" "That's how you know it's lucky." Devika shook her head and went off to fly the kite with the other kids. Yusuf muttered to his cousin that she was trying to trick him. But when he asked Salim at the shop what a top like his cost, Salim said, "Five rupees new, beta." Yusuf spun it again, and it wobbled.

qa.q: What did Devika offer for the top?
qa.a: Her new paper kite, with a long tail.

qa.q: Why does Yusuf think his chipped top is worth so much?
qa.a: He feels proud and attached because it is his, so even the chip seems lucky and valuable, and a fair offer feels like a trick.

qa.q: What small step would help Yusuf judge a fair trade?
qa.a: Asking himself whether he would give a kite and marbles to buy a top like his, especially after hearing Salim's price.

qa.q: How might Devika feel walking off with her kite?
qa.a: Devika may feel a little annoyed that her fair offer was called a trick, but happy to fly the kite anyway.

grounding: A boy prices his own chipped top far above what others would give and thinks a fair offer is a trick.

passage: At the school swap fair in Manchester, Wei set out his old comics on a blanket with a big sign: £5 EACH. Omar flipped through them. "These are good. I'll give you £1 each for the space ones." Wei looked shocked. "They're worth way more. I've read those twenty times." "That's why the corners are bent," Omar said. The comic stall next door had the same issues for 50p. By lunch Wei had sold nothing, and he told his mum the other kids were trying to rip him off. She held up one of the space comics. "Would you pay five pounds for this, if it was someone else's?" Wei looked at the bent corner for a long time.

qa.q: What did the next-door stall charge for the same comics?
Why did Wei think the other kids were trying to rip him off?
qa.a: He felt upset and insulted because the comics were his and read twenty times, so they felt worth far more than buyers offered.

qa.q: Why is Wei's mum's question useful?
qa.a: It makes Wei look at the comic as a buyer would, which shows the gap between what an owner feels and what others will pay.

qa.q: How does Omar see the comics?
qa.a: Omar likes them but sees bent corners and cheaper copies next door, so £1 seems a reasonable offer.

grounding: A boy prices his own comics far above what buyers will pay and believes they are trying to rip him off.

passage: Chen had written the first draft of the short film on a rainy weekend in Vancouver, and he loved every line of it. Nadia, his co-writer, came back on Monday with a second version: tighter, funnier, and the ending finally made sense. Their professor read both and circled Nadia's. "This one works." Chen felt his face go hot. "Mine has more heart," he said. "It's the original." He spent the week defending scenes that even he had yawned at, bringing back a long monologue Nadia had cut. On Friday, reading both aloud to the class, Chen heard his own draft drag. Nobody laughed where he had expected. He sat down and quietly admitted, "I think I liked it because it was mine."

qa.q: Which version did the professor circle?
qa.a: Nadia's.

qa.q: Why did Chen defend scenes he himself found dull?
qa.a: He felt protective and a bit hurt, because the draft was his original, so it felt more valuable than a better version.

qa.q: What could Chen try the next time he compares drafts?
qa.a: Read both aloud to a small group before deciding, or imagine someone else wrote both and judge which works better.

qa.q: What might that week have been like for Nadia?
qa.a: Nadia probably felt frustrated and awkward, seeing her cuts undone while trying not to hurt Chen.

grounding: A student clings to his own first draft over a better version, valuing it simply because it is his.

passage: The hostel's end-of-year sale filled the common room with mattresses, kettles and cycles. Imran had parked his old blue cycle by the door with a sign: 4,000 rupees. He had bought it three years ago for four and a half thousand. It had a squeaky chain and a bent mudguard, but it had carried him to every exam and to Ganga's birthday party in the rain. Three juniors looked at it and offered fifteen hundred. "Fifteen hundred? For this?" Imran said. "You don't know what it's been through." Ganga, the hostel secretary, checked the list: five other cycles were going for twelve to eighteen hundred. "If it were someone else's cycle, would you pay four thousand?" she asked. Imran looked at the bent mudguard and didn't answer.

qa.q: What price was on Imran's sign?
qa.a: 4,000 rupees.

qa.q: Why does Imran feel fifteen hundred is too little?
qa.a: He feels attached and a bit hurt, because the cycle carried him through three years of memories, so it seems worth far more than buyers see.

qa.q: What check does Ganga suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Asking whether he would pay four thousand if it were someone else's cycle, which lets him see its worth from a buyer's side.

qa.q: How do the juniors see the cycle?
qa.a: They see an old cycle with a squeaky chain and bent mudguard, worth about what the other cycles sell for.

grounding: A student prices his old cycle far above what similar cycles sell for, valuing it highly because it is his.

passage:
Dear Arohi,
I owe you an apology about the bridge model. When you suggested switching from my arch design to the truss, I argued for a whole week. I said the arch was more elegant, more "us." Honestly, it was more me. I had sketched it at 2 a.m. in first week, and I think I fell in love with it because it was mine.
Then on Thursday the load test cracked my arch at forty kilos. Your truss, which you built alone over the weekend, held sixty-five. I stood there feeling embarrassed and a bit silly.
I'd like us to go with the truss, and I'll do the write-up. Maybe I'll keep the arch sketch on my wall, as a reminder.
Harsha

qa.q: How much weight did Arohi's truss hold?
qa.a: Sixty-five kilos.

qa.q: Why did Harsha argue for the arch for a whole week?
qa.a: Harsha felt attached and proud, having sketched it at 2 a.m., so it seemed better simply because it was Harsha's own.

qa.q: What is Harsha doing to repair things with Arohi?
qa.a: Apologising honestly, choosing the truss and offering to do the write-up.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Arohi may feel relieved and respected, since the weekend of extra work is finally acknowledged.

grounding: A student writes an apology for defending an own design over a stronger alternative, valuing it because it was theirs.

passage: At the only mobile shop in the Shirpur market, Santosh put his old phone on the counter. "Twelve thousand," he said firmly. The shopkeeper turned it over, checked the battery, and said, "Five. Maybe five and a half." Santosh looked insulted. "I've kept it like new. Not one scratch. You people always cheat." Pooja, who shared the rented house with him and two other teachers, had come along to buy a charger. She waited until they were outside by the tea cart. "Santosh, if you walked in today to buy a two-year-old phone, what would you pay?" He started to answer, then stopped. "Six, maybe." "Then twelve is what it's worth to you. Not to the shop." Santosh laughed, a little embarrassed, and went back inside.

qa.q: What did the shopkeeper offer for the phone?
qa.a: Five, maybe five and a half.

qa.q: Why did Pooja wait until they were outside to speak?
qa.a: She seemed careful and kind, not wanting to embarrass Santosh in front of the shopkeeper while he felt insulted.

qa.q: What check did Pooja use, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked what he would pay to buy a two-year-old phone today, which made him see the price as a buyer does.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel when he goes back inside?
qa.a: He feels a little embarrassed but more open, ready to accept a price closer to what buyers pay.

grounding: A housemate watches a man price his used phone far above the shop's offer and asks what he would pay to buy one today.

passage: For two weeks Oskar's old phone sat in its box on the kitchen shelf of their Berlin flat, listed online for three hundred euros. Nkechi, his flatmate, watched him read the messages every evening. "One-fifty?" he would snort. "Do they know it has the good camera?" Listings for the same model all sat between one-forty and one-eighty, and Nkechi had seen them. On Sunday she made two coffees and put one beside him. "Quick question. If this exact phone was on someone else's listing for three hundred, would you buy it?" Oskar opened his mouth, then looked at his screen for a while. "I'd laugh at them," he admitted. "Then maybe ask one-seventy," Nkechi said, and he changed the price that night.

qa.q: What price range were other listings for the same model?
qa.a: Between one-forty and one-eighty.

qa.q: How did Nkechi probably feel watching Oskar each evening?
qa.a: She was probably amused but a little concerned, seeing him snort at fair offers night after night.

qa.q: Why did Nkechi's question work better than arguing about the price?
qa.a: It let Oskar picture himself as the buyer, so he saw the gap himself instead of being told.

qa.q: What changed for Oskar after the coffee conversation?
qa.a: He admitted he would laugh at a three-hundred listing and changed his price to a level buyers might accept.

grounding: A flatmate sees a man price his used phone far above what buyers offer and asks whether he would buy it at that price.

passage: Every morning Vishal ate the same thing: two rotis with jaggery, never anything else. Then he walked to the village school by the same path, past the temple, the well and the broken tractor, always on the left side. One Monday the path by the well was muddy, and his cousin Vijay pointed to the new cement road. "This way is shorter. And dry." Vishal stopped. "No. We go by the well." "Why?" "Because that's the way." He walked through the mud, his chappals squelching, and arrived late. At lunch Vijay offered him a bite of poha. Vishal shook his head. "I only eat rotis." "You've never even tried it." Vishal looked at the poha for a long time before he pushed it back.

qa.q: What did Vishal eat every morning?

qa.q: Why did Vishal walk through the mud instead of taking the dry road?
qa.a: He felt uneasy about changing, so the old muddy path felt safer than a new road, even though it made him late.

grounding: A boy sticks to the same breakfast and the same path even when a dry, shorter road and new food are fine.

passage: At the residential summer camp, the mess served something different each morning: dosa, upma, parathas. Pranav, eleven, took two slices of bread and jam every single day. He sat in the same corner chair, and he walked to the pool by the long path round the hall, even after the counsellor, Vidya ma'am, showed everyone the short cut through the garden. passage:
School counsellor's note, stream-change window, Class 11
Sahil came in today because his friend Suraj had switched from science to arts last week and "looked so happy it was annoying." Sahil is in science because, as he put it, "everyone in my house did science, so I just did." When I asked what he would have chosen on a blank page, he said history, then laughed nervously. He listed reasons to stay: the tuition already paid, the group chat, the forms, what his mother would say. None of the reasons were about liking science. I told him the window closes on the 20th and that staying is also a choice he is allowed to make, as long as it is a choice. He will talk to his mother this weekend and come back on Monday.

qa.q: When does the stream-change window close?
qa.a: On the 20th.

qa.q: Why did Sahil laugh nervously after saying history?
qa.a: He felt nervous and a little exposed, because saying it out loud showed that science was a default he never truly chose.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped Sahil?
qa.a: Asked what he would choose on a blank page, noticed his reasons weren't about liking science, and gave a clear deadline and next step.

qa.q: How does Suraj seem after switching?
qa.a: Suraj seems so happy that Sahil finds it annoying, which suggests the switch suited him.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenage boy who is in the family's stream by default and has listed only effort-based reasons to stay.

passage:
Academic adviser's note, second-year advising, 12 August
Ishita came for her elective sign-off. For the third semester in a row she has chosen the basic spreadsheet course, now at level 2, taught from the same slides. When I asked why, she said, "It's fine, I'm used to it." Her friend Jasleen, who took the data design elective, had told her it was hard but "finally interesting." Ishita admitted she had read that syllabus and liked it, but switching meant a new timetable, new classmates and a waitlist form. "Honestly, I'm content where I am," she said, looking at the floor. I showed her the waitlist form: one page, due Friday. She took it with her. I will check with her on Friday.

qa.q: Which elective did Jasleen take?
qa.a: The data design elective.

qa.q: What does Ishita looking at the floor suggest about her content answer?
qa.a: It suggests she may feel less content than she says, perhaps bored or uneasy, and is staying mainly because switching feels like effort.

qa.q: What did the adviser make easier, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Showing her the one-page waitlist form due Friday, which makes switching less effort so a real choice becomes possible.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel if Ishita joins the data design elective?
qa.a: Jasleen would probably feel glad to have her friend in a class she finds finally interesting.

grounding: An adviser records a student staying in a weak course because switching takes effort, while calling it contentment.

passage:
Sunday night
Realised today I've studied in bed every night for two years, laptop on my knees, and I fall asleep by page three every single time. Hafsa goes to the reading room on the second floor at seven. She finishes in two hours what takes me four.
She asked me again tonight, "Come with me?" I said, "Nah, I'm comfortable here." And I am comfortable. That's the problem. It's not that I love the bed. It's that going means shoes, a bag, a walk, finding a seat. Changing feels like a whole project, so I tell myself I'm happy.
Tomorrow: shoes by the door at 6:45. Just one night. If it's awful, fine.
Jaya

qa.q: Why is shoes by the door at 6:45, just one night, a good plan?
qa.a: It makes the change tiny and easy to start, so effort no longer hides behind feeling content.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel if Jaya finally comes along?
qa.a: Hafsa would probably feel pleased, since she keeps inviting Jaya to the reading room.

grounding: A student's diary shows a weak study habit kept only because changing takes effort, dressed up as being comfortable.
